title: Grandparents
hookLine: the tradition prizes the link between grandparents and grandchildren
tomorrow: Joseph's brothers sold him. so how does that story end?

lines: WHAT ONLY A GRANDPARENT HANDS DOWN?
cards: A grandparent's phone, or their shoebox, is full of photos of you that you've never seen. Blurry ones. Ones from before you could remember.
Proof of a life you were already part of. So, one question for today: what does a grandparent hand down that a parent can't?

teach.b: Deuteronomy tucks an answer inside a warning. Don't forget what your eyes saw, it says, but "make them known unto thy children and thy children's children." Two generations, named in one breath.

teach.h: TEACH A GRANDCHILD: AS IF AT SINAI.
teach.b: The Talmud, in Kiddushin, reads it boldly: whoever teaches a grandchild Torah, scripture treats it as if they had received it at Mount Sinai. The grandparent stands at the mountain again, handing it on.
So here's the tradition's answer: a grandparent hands down memory with proof attached. Three generations at one table are a chain you can see. And a neighbor says something close.
In the Christian New Testament, Paul writes to young Timothy, in the King James words: "the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice."
A grandmother, named in scripture, as the place a faith first lived. Jews and Christians both keep that picture: faith in a household, passed down by name.

One honest difference: for Paul, what Lois handed on was faith in Christ. For the Talmud, what a grandparent hands on is Torah, traced back to Sinai. The same chain of hands, carrying different things.

how: Jewish grandparents may take part in a grandchild's milestones: holding the baby at a brit milah or a naming, teaching a holiday song, standing beside them at a bar or bat mitzvah; in some families a child is named for a grandparent.

o: the elders who lead prayers in a synagogue
the generation that links you to the one before
the parents of a newly married couple

games.q: a chain of hands — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah speaks only of parents teaching children
the Talmud compares teaching a grandchild to receiving Torah at Sinai
Jews and Christians pass down exactly the same thing through grandparents
both honor the chain; Paul speaks of faith in Christ, the Talmud of Torah.

games.q: your grandfather starts the same old story at dinner again, and your kids roll their eyes. with Deuteronomy 4:9 in mind, what do you do?
o: let him tell it; the children's children are the ones meant to hear it.
ask him to save it for a holiday, when there's more time.
record it once, so nobody has to hear it at dinner again.
games.why: Deuteronomy wants what the eyes saw made known to children and their children. the retelling is the handing on.

practice: Count three things an older person handed you: a recipe, a saying, a way of folding a shirt, a story about your family from before you were born. Stay with each one for a few breaths.
If your grandparents are gone, let at least one of the three be theirs.

wordCard.voice: Grandparents: the second link in the chain, and in the Talmud's reading, a way back to Sinai.

orig.note: Hebrew (from Aramaic): grandfather; savta is grandmother.

carryVoice: For today: three generations, each handing on what it was handed. A full week of home and family.
